_meta.title: Base verbs and their complement frames
_meta.description: A finite inventory of common English verbs in base form, each tagged with the complement frames it can take. Answers two different questions that no other file here answers: (1) is this word a verb at all - which pure suffix analysis cannot decide, since 'conduct' and 'plan' carry no inflection and '-s' is ambiguous between plural noun and third-person verb; and (2) what does this verb license - whether it can take an object, two objects, a clause, or none. Frames are the fact that lets a consumer reject a reading in which an intransitive verb has been given a direct object.
_meta.source_notes: Complement frames (subcategorization) are a standard descriptive category in English grammar; the six used here are the conventional teaching set. The gf_category field records the corresponding category name in Grammatical Framework's Resource Grammar Library, purely as an interoperability key - names of grammatical categories are not copyrightable and no GF code or data is used or derived from here. Recorded because GF's own engine is GPL-3.0 while its RGL is dual LGPL/BSD: if this project ever needs its own framework, this inventory should carry over unchanged.
_meta.status: seed - common core plus the copula/auxiliary set and common science-register verbs. Incomplete by design and expected to grow; a verb's absence means unknown, never 'not a verb'.
_meta.framework_independence: Deliberately engine-neutral. Frames are named in plain descriptive terms, with the GF category recorded alongside rather than instead. Nothing here assumes a parser, a formalism, or a programming language.
_meta.see_also: irregular-verbs.json holds the FORMS of verbs whose past is not -ed. This file holds what verbs COMBINE WITH. The two overlap in membership and neither subsumes the other: 'grow' appears in both, 'conduct' only here, and a verb may be irregular yet unremarkable in its frames.

fields.collective: Optional boolean, default false. The verb's action is inherently joint: 'Apple and Microsoft merged' does NOT entail 'Apple merged'. This is the fact that forbids distributing a compound subject into separate propositions; absence of the flag on a listed verb means the verb distributes, while an UNLISTED verb licenses nothing (open world). Ambiguous verbs (e.g. 'gather', collective intransitively but distributive with an object) are left unflagged rather than half-claimed.

_provenance._note:
Who added what, when, and how. Recorded per BATCH rather than per entry: the data was created in batches, so batch records are honest and stay readable, while an entry needing individual sourcing (a teacher contribution, a single corrected form) may carry its own `prov` field.

Batches are identified by DATE and COMMIT SUBJECT, deliberately not by commit hash. A hash means nothing to a human auditor and breaks the moment history is ever rewritten; a subject line is stable, readable, and findable with `git log --grep`.

`method` is the load-bearing field. `authored` = compiled from facts by a person. `mined` = derived by code from a corpus named in PROVENANCE.md. `assistant` = drafted by an AI assistant at the maintainer's direction and accepted by the maintainer. All three produce uncopyrightable facts, so none affects the free-forever promise; recording which is which lets a downstream user filter and keeps the chain auditable by someone who was not here.

intransitive.gloss: Takes a subject and no object. "Costs rose."

transitive.gloss: Takes a subject and one direct object. "Students conduct investigations."

ditransitive.gloss: Takes two objects. "The company gave shareholders a dividend."

clausal.gloss: Takes a that-clause as its complement. "The report says that revenue increased."

linking.gloss: Links the subject to a complement rather than acting on an object. "The results are significant."

verb_complement.gloss: Takes another verb as its complement. "Students plan to investigate."

avalent.gloss: Takes no argument at all — the weather/impersonal verbs. "It rains." The subject 'it' is a grammatical placeholder (an expletive), not an actant.
